sentences.text: Callisto, the outermost and quietest of the four Galilean moons.
Its surface is the most densely cratered surface in the Solar System; it has hardly changed in 4 billion years.
Because it is far from Jupiter, it is unaffected by tidal heating and remains outside the radiation belts.
That makes it the safest candidate for a future crewed base; there are also hints that an ocean may lie beneath it as well.
Europa, the most promising destination in the search for life.
It is a little smaller than our Moon; but beneath its smooth ice shell, a global ocean is thought to exist, holding twice as much water as all the oceans on Earth.
The brown lines on the surface are places where the ice has cracked and water from below has seeped up.
NASA's Europa Clipper spacecraft was launched in 2024, and in 2030 it will investigate, with about 50 close flybys, whether this ocean is habitable.
Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System.
It is even larger than the planet Mercury; when we place them side by side, you can see this.
It is the only known moon with its own magnetic field; this field forms a small bubble inside Jupiter's and creates auroras at its poles.
Its surface is of two different ages: dark, cratered ancient regions and light-colored, grooved younger regions.
It too has an ocean beneath its ice shell; the European Space Agency's JUICE spacecraft will enter orbit around it in 2031.
Io, the most volcanic world in the Solar System.
It is constantly squeezed and stretched between the gravity of Jupiter and the other moons; this tidal heating melts its interior.
There are more than 400 active volcanoes on its surface, and some hurl lava hundreds of kilometers high; the largest, Loki Patera, is a lava lake 200 kilometers across.
The yellow, orange, and red colors come from sulfur and sulfur compounds.
Its surface is renewed so quickly that there are almost no impact craters on it.
Finally, let's look at Juno: this NASA spacecraft entered orbit around Jupiter in July 2016.
It is the first spacecraft to operate on solar power this far from the Sun; its three giant panels take up as much space as a basketball court.
To protect itself from radiation, it travels in a long, elliptical orbit passing over the poles; here is that orbit, sped up.
On each pass it flies a few thousand kilometers above the clouds and discovered giant cyclones at Jupiter's poles.
It showed that the core is larger and more diffuse than had been thought.
It has been a journey from Galileo's four tiny points of light to worlds hiding oceans beneath their ice.
Perhaps the place to look for life in the Solar System is not near a warming sun, but on these cold, dark moons kneaded by a giant's gravity.
Our tour of Jupiter ends here.
A bright, steady light in the night sky: to the naked eye, no different from an ordinary star.

Yet the owner of that light is a giant two and a half times heavier than all the other planets combined; an architect that bends the paths of comets with its gravity and has shaped the order of the Solar System for billions of years.
Welcome to the Jupiter system; this giant is almost like a small solar system.
More than 95 moons orbit around it; let's watch the orbits of the four largest from above.

Io completes one orbit in 2 days, Europa in three and a half days, Ganymede in 7 days, and Callisto in 17 days; the inner three are locked together, and when Io completes 4 orbits, Europa completes 2 and Ganymede 1.
The planet is so large that 1,300 Earths would fit inside it, and its magnetic field is the largest structure in the Solar System.
In 1610, Galileo discovered these four moons with his small telescope; it was the first evidence that not everything revolves around Earth.
Now we will visit those four moons in turn.
